invite verb and noun

also invitation, invited, ask someone to dinner, ask someone round, have someone over

classical

Cic. Off. 3.59: invītat Canius postrīdiē familiārēs suōs
Cic. Att. 5.1.3
Traupman 334

invītō, invītāre, invītāvī, invītātum

verb, first conjugation, transitive: aliquem ad cēnam, in hospitium, domum invītāre

The general word, with ad or in and the accusative, with domum, or with ut and the subjunctive (Cic. Att. 13.2, Lewis & Short). Things invite too, “tempt, attract” (Lucr. 5.524). Not to be confused with invītus, “unwilling”.

Other words

  • vocō, vocāre, vocāvī, vocātum — ask (to a meal)

    verb, first conjugation, transitive: ad cēnam vocāre · also used · classical · Ter. And. 2.6.22: ad cēnam (Lewis & Short); Cic. Att. 6.3.9 (Lewis & Short); Traupman 334: “(esp. to dinner) vocāre”

    Its first sense is “call, summon”; asking someone to a meal was simply vocāre, and the invited guest is vocātus (Lewis & Short, s.v. vocō, “to bid, invite one as a guest”).

  • invītātiō, invītātiōnis f. — an invitation

    noun, third declension · also used · classical · Cic. Att. 9.12.1: in Ēpīrum invītātiō quam suāvis! (Lewis & Short); Cic. Phil. 9.6 (Lewis & Short)

Examples

  • Pompōnia, inquit, tū invītā mulierēs, ego virōs accīverō

    “Pomponia,” he said, “you invite the women, and I’ll have fetched the men.”Cic. Att. 5.1.3

  • invītat Canius postrīdiē familiārēs suōs

    the next day Canius invites his friendsCic. Off. 3.59

  • Quam vellem Menedēmum invītātum ut nōbīscum esset hodiē amplius

    How I wish Menedemus had been invited, to be with us today as wellTer. Heaut. 185

See also guest, visitor, host, receive, visit, party.

SourcesLewis & Short: invito · Lewis & Short: voco · Lewis & Short: invitatio
